patients.summary: Retired accountant who joins the practice at 70 with hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, a remote stroke and alcohol use disorder in early remission. Over the next decade he develops presbycusis, aortic stenosis, multi-infarct dementia, locally advanced prostate cancer on androgen deprivation, a Zenker diverticulum, central cord syndrome after a fall, and in June 2026 an acute subdural hematoma that is evacuated. Outside records are patchy; his daughter carries much of the communication.

documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
NEW PATIENT VISIT

70-year-old retired accountant transferring care; wanted a practice where he could reach the doctor directly. Lives alone in Easthampton. Prior primary care elsewhere for years; records release signed today.

HISTORY
- Hypertension since roughly 2005, on hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily. Home cuff readings he recalls in the 130s.
- Type 2 diabetes since about 2009, metformin 500 mg twice daily. Last A1c he remembers was 'under 7'. No hypoglycemia. No foot sores.
- High cholesterol, atorvastatin 20 mg at night, no muscle complaints.
- Neck: long-standing stiffness, told years ago it was arthritis of the neck (cervical spondylosis). No arm numbness or weakness. Uses heat, nothing else.
- Hay fever in spring and late summer, loratadine when needed.
- Stroke around 2011. Vague on details: was in the hospital a couple of days, 'it all came back' within weeks. No deficits he is aware of.
- Alcohol: describes years of heavy drinking that he calls a problem; stopped completely in late November and has not had a drink since. Going to meetings. Wants it on his record so we can help him stay on track.

SURGICAL: none.
ALLERGIES: none to medications.
FAMILY: father had coronary disease and a narrowed aortic valve; mother had Alzheimer disease late in life; older brother treated for prostate cancer.
SOCIAL: never used tobacco. No other substances. Retired from accounting. Drives. Has a daughter who lives nearby.

ROS: no chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations, bowel or urinary trouble, weight change, mood complaints.

EXAM
Vitals per flowsheet. Well appearing, pleasant, a bit hard of hearing when I turned away.
HEENT: canals clear, oropharynx normal. Neck: supple, reduced rotation both directions, no bruits, no thyromegaly.
Heart: regular rate and rhythm. Lungs: clear throughout.
Abdomen: soft, nontender. Ext: no edema; feet intact skin, monofilament sensation normal, pulses 2+.
Neuro: alert and oriented, fluent, strength 5/5 throughout, gait steady.

ASSESSMENT / PLAN
1. Hypertension: near goal on HCTZ. Continue; recheck with BMP.
2. Type 2 diabetes: metformin continued. A1c, urine microalbumin today. Eye exam with his optometrist yearly.
3. Hyperlipidemia: atorvastatin 20 continued. Lipids today.
4. Remote stroke, recovered: on statin. Will review old records when they come.
5. Alcohol use disorder, early remission: encouraged, meetings, he knows he can call. AUDIT-C 0 for the past weeks.
6. Cervical spondylosis, allergic rhinitis: stable.
7. Health maintenance: hepatitis C screen today. Colonoscopy and vaccines per old records. Wellness visit in spring.

Return in about 6 months, sooner as needed.

documents.title: Your lab results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Mr. Fleming,

Your blood work from the 10th is back. Kidney function, potassium, blood counts and thyroid are normal. A1c is right around 7, which is reasonable for you. LDL cholesterol is under 100 on the atorvastatin. Urine protein is normal and the hepatitis C screen is negative.

No changes. See you in the spring for your wellness visit.

Your primary care physician

- 2011 hospital discharge summary: minor ischemic stroke, symptoms resolved before discharge; discharged on his usual medications.
- Medication list matches ours: HCTZ 25, metformin 500 twice daily, atorvastatin 20, loratadine as needed.
- No drug allergies listed.

Routed to PCP for review.

documents.title: Hearing
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
CC: hearing.

He is ready to have his hearing looked at. Over the last few years it has slowly gotten harder to follow conversation, worst at his meetings and in restaurants where there is background noise. Turns the TV up. No ear pain, drainage, ringing he notices, or spinning. Never worked around loud machinery; no gunfire. No new medications.

Exam: external canals clear, tympanic membranes normal both sides. Misses several whispered words on each side. Rest of exam not repeated today.

A/P:
1. Gradual bilateral hearing loss, likely age related. ENT/audiology referral placed.
2. Diabetes: A1c drawn today since he was due; yearly labs at the January visit.

reports.text: Pure-tone audiometry, both ears. Thresholds normal to mildly reduced through 1000 Hz, sloping to a moderate-to-severe loss at 3000 to 8000 Hz bilaterally, symmetric. Air-bone gaps absent. Speech reception thresholds agree with pure-tone averages; word recognition reduced in quiet, worse with competing noise. Tympanometry type A both ears.
reports.conclusion: Bilateral symmetric high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss.

documents.title: Otolaryngology consultation
documents.author: otolaryngology
documents.body:
OTOLARYNGOLOGY CONSULTATION
Date of visit: 12/31/2018
Referred by: primary care

Thank you for sending Mr. Fleming, 72, for hearing loss. He describes a slow decline over several years; noisy rooms are the hardest. He has had no otalgia, otorrhea or vertigo. He reports no occupational or recreational noise exposure and has taken no ototoxic medications.

PMH: hypertension, type 2 diabetes, hyperlipidemia, cervical spondylosis, seasonal allergic rhinitis, prior stroke, alcohol use disorder.
MEDICATIONS: hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily, metformin 500 mg twice daily, atorvastatin 20 mg at bedtime, loratadine 10 mg as needed.
ALLERGIES: NKDA.
FAMILY: father CAD and aortic stenosis; mother Alzheimer disease; brother prostate cancer.
SOCIAL: never smoker. Alcohol use disorder, sober about two years. Retired accountant.

EXAM: auricles and canals normal; tympanic membranes intact and mobile. He could not repeat whispered words at 2 feet. Tuning fork: Weber midline, Rinne positive (air conduction greater than bone) on both sides. Nose and oral cavity unremarkable.

AUDIOGRAM: bilateral high-frequency sensorineural loss, symmetric (report attached).

IMPRESSION: Presbycusis, bilateral.

PLAN: no imaging needed for a symmetric pattern. Referred to our audiologists for a hearing aid evaluation. Communication strategies reviewed. Repeat audiogram in 1 to 2 years or with any sudden change.

Otolaryngology

documents.title: Dyspnea on exertion
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
CC: getting winded.

HPI: Since around Labor Day he has been more short of breath with exertion. Climbing the stairs to his daughter's apartment leaves him tired and he has to stop halfway. Walking up the hill on his usual route he sometimes feels lightheaded and stops until it passes. Has had a mild pressure-type discomfort in the chest on a couple of those walks, gone with rest. Has cut his walks short. No symptoms at rest, no fainting, no orthopnea, no leg swelling, no cough.

EXAM: vitals per flowsheet; comfortable at rest.
Heart: regular. Harsh systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border.
Lungs: clear. Ext: no edema.

ECG: sinus rhythm, no acute changes.

A/P: Exertional dyspnea, presyncope and chest discomfort with a new-to-me harsh basal systolic murmur. Concern for a valve lesion, given his father's history too. CBC and BMP today. Cardiology referral, asked for a prompt appointment, with echocardiogram. Told him to avoid strenuous exertion until seen and to call 911 for chest pain that does not settle or for fainting.

reports.text: Left ventricle normal in size with normal wall thickness pattern and normal regional wall motion. Visually estimated LVEF 60%. Aortic valve heavily calcified with reduced excursion of the leaflets. Mitral valve structurally normal. Right ventricle normal in size and function. Atria normal size. No pericardial effusion. Aortic root normal.
reports.conclusion: Heavily calcified aortic valve with reduced leaflet excursion consistent with aortic stenosis. Normal LV systolic function, LVEF 60%.

documents.title: Cardiology consultation
documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
CARDIOLOGY CONSULTATION
Visit: 01/10/2020

Dear Doctor,

I saw Mr. Fleming, 73, at your request. For about three months he has noticed breathlessness and fatigue going up stairs and occasional lightheadedness walking uphill. He also describes mild chest discomfort and says he has to rest more during his day. This comes about a year after his ENT evaluation for hearing loss.

History: hypertension, well controlled on a thiazide; type 2 diabetes; hyperlipidemia; prior stroke; presbycusis.
Medications: hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily, metformin 500 mg twice daily, atorvastatin 20 mg at bedtime, loratadine 10 mg as needed.
Allergies: none known.
Family history: father with coronary disease and aortic stenosis.
Social: never smoked; sober about two years from alcohol; retired accountant.

Exam: pulse slow and regular. Second heart sound soft. Harsh, late-peaking systolic murmur loudest at the upper right sternal border with him sitting up. Carotid upstrokes are slow and reduced in volume. Lungs clear. No edema.

Echo today: heavily calcified aortic valve with restricted leaflet motion; LV ejection fraction 60%.

Impression: calcific aortic valve stenosis with exertional symptoms; preserved LV function.

Plan: return to see me in 6 months with a repeat echocardiogram, sooner if symptoms change. Avoid heavy exertion. Continue current medications. Call with any syncope or rest symptoms.

Cardiology

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, high MDM

documents.title: Memory concerns
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Seen with his daughter.

HPI: Daughter describes about two months of decline: bills piling up, trouble following recipes he has cooked for years, the stove left on, and getting lost on a familiar drive last week. More short-tempered. He minimizes it ('everyone forgets'). New today: the daughter says that in January he told her his left arm and leg felt weak and clumsy for several days; he did not call anyone and 'it mostly got better'. He confirms this, vague on dates, thinks around the third week of January. No headache, no falls, no alcohol (daughter agrees).

EXAM: vitals per flowsheet. Alert, cooperative, repeats questions. Speech fluent. Left arm drifts; left grip and left hip flexion weaker than right. Left reflexes livelier than right. Gait a little wide, no falls in clinic. Mini-Cog: 1 of 3 words, clock with numbers crowded on one side. Heart: basal systolic murmur as before. Lungs clear.

A/P:
1. Subacute cognitive decline, with the history of a second, unreported stroke in January and residual left-sided weakness. Labs today (B12, TSH, CMP, CBC) for reversible causes. Neurology referral, expedited.
2. Left hemiparesis after stroke (January 2021): added to problem list.
3. Safety: no driving for now; he agreed reluctantly, daughter will take the keys. Stove: daughter looking into an automatic shut-off. Daughter will check in daily.
4. Chronic issues unchanged; meds as before. Daughter will review pill organizer.

documents.title: Lab results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: George (and your daughter, who you said may read these): the blood tests we did for memory came back normal, including B12, thyroid, salt and calcium levels, kidney function and blood counts. Nothing there explains the memory change, so the neurology visit is the next step. Their office has the referral.

documents.title: Neurology consultation
documents.author: neurology
documents.body:
NEUROLOGY CONSULTATION
Date of service: 07/07/2021

Reason: cognitive decline.

Mr. Fleming, 75, comes with his daughter, who has noticed worsening memory and a change in personality over about two months. He is having difficulty with things that used to be easy, such as keeping his bills in order and cooking; recently he left the stove on unattended and lost his way driving to a nearby store. This is in the setting of earlier cerebrovascular disease and known aortic stenosis. He had a small stroke roughly six months ago, not evaluated at the time, and has residual left-sided weakness. Other history includes type 2 diabetes, hyperlipidemia, long-standing hypertension, presbycusis.

Medications: hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily, metformin 500 mg twice daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, loratadine 10 mg as needed.
Allergies: NKDA.
Social: lives by himself and now needs regular supervision. Does not drink or smoke.

Exam: BP 150/88, pulse 76. Cranial nerves II to XII intact. Power 3/5 in the left arm and leg, normal on the right. Reflexes brisker on the left; left plantar extensor. MMSE 24/30. Delayed recall 1 of 3 at five minutes.

Impression: multi-infarct (vascular) dementia, with a stepwise course in the setting of two clinical strokes and vascular risk factors.

Recommendations:
- Supervision for finances, medications and cooking; no driving.
- Continue control of blood pressure, glucose and lipids per primary care.
- Follow up in neurology in 6 months.

Neurology

Plan: A1c and BMP today. Meds unchanged. Neurology follow-up in January per their plan. RTC 5 months; daughter has portal proxy access.

documents.title: Urology consultation
documents.author: urology
documents.body:
UROLOGY NEW PATIENT CONSULTATION
Visit date: 01/04/2023

Mr. Fleming is a 76-year-old man with hypertension, type 2 diabetes, prior stroke and multi-infarct dementia, accompanied by his daughter, referred for urinary symptoms and an elevated PSA. He has to strain to begin voiding, the stream is intermittent, and he gets up several times a night. He notes a dull lower abdominal discomfort. No flank pain, gross hematuria or fevers. Appetite is preserved but he has lost weight over the last few months without trying.

PMH: as above, plus aortic stenosis and presbycusis. No previous urologic procedures or surgery.
Meds: hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg, metformin 500 mg twice daily, atorvastatin 20 mg, loratadine as needed.
Allergies: NKDA.
Family history: older brother with prostate cancer.
Social: never smoker.

Exam: abdomen soft, no masses, bladder not palpable. DRE: prostate hard and irregular with nodularity.

Data: PSA 48.6 (11/2022, primary care), markedly elevated.

Assessment: findings highly suspicious for prostate cancer.

Plan: multiparametric prostate MRI, then transrectal biopsy. Discussed with patient and daughter, who agree. Will see them after biopsy.

Urology

documents.title: Urology letter
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Urology consult received. Suspicious exam; MRI and biopsy being arranged.

documents.title: MRI prostate with and without contrast
documents.author: radiology
documents.body:
MRI PROSTATE, MULTIPARAMETRIC (performed 01/19/2023)
Indication: PSA 48.6, abnormal DRE.

Findings: enlarged prostate. A large lesion in the peripheral zone with marked restricted diffusion and early enhancement. Tumor extends through the prostatic capsule and into the adjacent seminal vesicles. Bladder wall and rectum are preserved. No enlarged pelvic lymph nodes. No suspicious marrow lesions in the imaged pelvis.

Impression: findings of prostate cancer with extracapsular extension into the seminal vesicles.

reports.text:
Specimen: prostate, transrectal ultrasound-guided needle biopsies, 12 cores (sextant bilateral, medial and lateral).
Microscopic: prostatic adenocarcinoma, acinar type, present in 8 of 12 cores. Gleason score 4+4=8 (Grade Group 4).
reports.conclusion: Prostatic adenocarcinoma, Gleason 4+4=8 (Grade Group 4), 8 of 12 cores.

documents.title: Prostate biopsy
documents.author: urology
documents.body:
PROCEDURE: transrectal ultrasound-guided prostate biopsy, 12 cores, 01/24/2023, under local block with prophylactic antibiotic. Daughter present for consent; patient assented and understood the procedure. Tolerated well, no immediate complications. Discharged home.

Pathology: adenocarcinoma, Gleason 4+4=8, Grade Group 4, 8 of 12 cores. Staging CT abdomen/pelvis and bone scan ordered; return visit to discuss treatment.

Urology

documents.title: Biopsy results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: MRI and pathology reports in today. Called daughter; urology had already told them it is cancer. Reviewed in plain terms: high-grade prostate cancer that has grown just outside the gland; staging scans next; treatment is usually hormone therapy with or without radiation and urology will go through it. She asked whether his dementia changes anything; told her it is part of choosing the gentlest effective plan and that we will support whatever they decide. Problem list updated.

reports.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast
reports.text: Liver, spleen, pancreas, adrenal glands and kidneys normal. No hydronephrosis. No enlarged retroperitoneal or pelvic lymph nodes. Prostate enlarged. Bladder normally distended. No ascites. No lytic or blastic bone lesions. Mild degenerative change of the lumbar spine.
reports.conclusion: No lymphadenopathy or osseous metastatic disease.

documents.title: Bone scan
documents.author: radiology
documents.body:
WHOLE-BODY BONE SCAN (02/07/2023)
Indication: newly diagnosed prostate adenocarcinoma.
Findings: physiologic tracer distribution. Mild uptake at the lower cervical spine and knees consistent with degenerative change. No pattern of metastatic disease.
Impression: no scintigraphic evidence of osseous metastases.

medications.sig: Take 1 tablet by mouth daily for 4 weeks
22.5 mg intramuscularly every 3 months, given in urology office; first dose 2/28/2023

documents.title: Urology follow-up: treatment plan
documents.author: urology
documents.body:
UROLOGY FOLLOW-UP
Visit date: 02/14/2023

Seen with daughter (health care proxy) to review results.
Pathology: adenocarcinoma, Gleason 4+4=8 (Grade Group 4), 8/12 cores. MRI: extracapsular extension into seminal vesicles. CT abdomen/pelvis: no adenopathy, no bone lesions. Bone scan negative.

Assessment: locally advanced, nonmetastatic high-risk prostate cancer.

Discussion: options of androgen deprivation with radiation versus androgen deprivation alone. Given his age, vascular dementia and wish to avoid daily treatment trips, patient and daughter prefer androgen deprivation alone with close PSA follow-up. Side effects reviewed: hot flashes, fatigue, weight and muscle change, glucose effects, bone thinning.

Plan:
- Bicalutamide 50 mg daily for 4 weeks, starting today.
- Leuprolide 22.5 mg IM every 3 months, first injection 2/28.
- PSA in 3 months.

Urology

EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT PHYSICIAN NOTE
Date of service: 01/03/2024

CC: cannot pass urine.

HPI: 77-year-old man brought by his daughter. Lower abdominal pain and no urine output for the last 24 hours. Followed by urology for suspected prostate cancer; a year of gradually weaker stream and nighttime voiding. Two days ago he began a nonprescription allergy tablet that he had heard might help his symptoms; daughter did not bring the box.

PMH: hypertension on hydrochlorothiazide, seasonal allergic rhinitis, diabetes, dementia, prior stroke, aortic stenosis.
Meds (per daughter): metformin 500 mg twice daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, loratadine 10 mg as needed, hydrochlorothiazide, the OTC allergy product.
Allergies: NKDA.

Exam: BP 145/90, HR 78. Uncomfortable. Lower abdomen distended with a palpable, tender bladder. DRE: prostate enlarged, smooth and firm. Mucous membranes dry. No new focal neurological deficit.

Labs: creatinine 1.2, BUN 19, potassium 4.5, sodium 140.

Course: urethral catheter placed with prompt relief and a large volume drained. Comfortable afterward.

Impression: acute urinary retention, likely the OTC allergy medication on top of prostatic obstruction.

Disposition: home with indwelling catheter and leg bag. Stop the OTC allergy product. Urology for voiding trial within a week. Return for fever, catheter blockage or bleeding.

Emergency Medicine

documents.title: Gastroenterology consultation
documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
GASTROENTEROLOGY CONSULTATION
Date of visit: 12/27/2024

Thank you for referring Mr. Fleming, a 78-year-old man with multi-infarct dementia, prostate cancer on hormone therapy, aortic valve stenosis and prior strokes, seen with his daughter. For six months he has had on-and-off difficulty swallowing, mostly solids, and nighttime regurgitation of food that comes back undigested. He describes a lump in the throat and his daughter notes persistent bad breath. He was treated with antibiotics for pneumonia twice in the past year.

Medications: hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily, metformin 500 mg twice daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, loratadine 10 mg as needed, leuprolide every 3 months.
Allergies: NKDA.
Social: never smoker; long abstinent from alcohol.

Exam: small, soft, nontender, compressible fullness in the left side of the neck. No cervical lymphadenopathy. Abdomen benign.

Impression: history and exam suggest a pharyngoesophageal (Zenker) diverticulum with aspiration.

Plan: barium swallow, then review. Meanwhile, upright for 2 hours after meals, small bites, soft diet.

Gastroenterology

documents.title: GI letter
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: GI consult received. Suspected Zenker diverticulum; barium swallow scheduled.

documents.title: Barium swallow
documents.author: radiology
documents.body:
BARIUM ESOPHAGRAM (01/08/2025)
Indication: solid dysphagia, regurgitation, recurrent pneumonia.

Technique: single-contrast thin and thick barium swallow in frontal and lateral projections.

Findings: posterior outpouching arising just above the cricopharyngeus at the pharyngoesophageal junction, about 3 cm, filling with and retaining barium after the swallow. The cervical esophagus below it and the thoracic esophagus have normal caliber and motility. No stricture or mass. Gastroesophageal junction unremarkable. No aspiration observed during the study.

Impression: Zenker diverticulum, approximately 3 cm, with barium retention. Esophagus otherwise normal.

documents.title: Esophagram
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Barium swallow: 3 cm Zenker diverticulum. Added to problem list. GI will discuss treatment.

documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
PROCEDURE: flexible endoscopic Zenker diverticulotomy (septotomy), 02/18/2025
Indication: symptomatic 3 cm Zenker diverticulum with recurrent aspiration pneumonia.
Sedation: monitored anesthesia care.

Findings: diverticulum at the pharyngoesophageal junction with a cricopharyngeal septum. Septum divided with a needle-knife to near the base; clips placed at the apex. Esophagus beyond normal. No bleeding or perforation.

Post-procedure: observed, tolerated clear liquids that afternoon, discharged home with his daughter. Liquids for 2 days, then soft foods for a week, then regular diet as tolerated.

documents.title: Hospital discharge summary
documents.author: hospital medicine
documents.body:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admitted: 06/26/2025 via ED. Discharged: 07/01/2025 to inpatient rehabilitation.

Presentation: 79-year-old man with cervical spondylosis, prior strokes and multi-infarct dementia, treated six months ago for a Zenker diverticulum. Early this morning he lost his balance in the bathroom and hit his chin on the sink, without loss of consciousness. Afterward he could not use his hands well and felt clumsy doing up buttons, with a burning feeling over his shoulders and upper arms. He denied neck pain, leg weakness, and any change in bladder or bowel function.

Exam in ED: strength 4/5 in both arms, weaker in the hands than at the shoulders; legs 5/5. Pain and temperature sensation reduced over the shoulders and arms on both sides; vibration and joint position sense preserved.

Imaging: CT head without acute findings (old infarcts). CT cervical spine: no fracture or malalignment; multilevel degenerative spondylosis. MRI cervical spine: multilevel spondylotic canal narrowing, most marked at C4-C5, with cord edema at that level; no ligamentous injury or epidural collection.

Diagnosis: central cord syndrome after a fall, on a background of cervical spondylosis.

Course: neurosurgery consulted; nonoperative management recommended. Soft collar for comfort. Blood pressure kept in a good range. PT/OT daily; hand function and burning pain improving by discharge. No bladder retention.

Medications at discharge: unchanged home medications (hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg, metformin 500 mg twice daily, atorvastatin 20 mg, loratadine as needed, leuprolide per urology).
Allergies: NKDA.

Disposition: inpatient rehabilitation. Neurosurgery clinic in 6 weeks. PCP follow-up after rehab.

Hospital Medicine

documents.body: Discharge summary in: central cord syndrome, nonoperative. In rehab now. Problem list updated.

documents.title: Daughter: fall, admitted
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Daughter called: he fell in the bathroom yesterday morning, hit his chin, and could not use his hands properly. ED said a bruised spinal cord in the neck from arthritis plus the fall, no surgery for now. Admitted. Expected to go to rehab. Message to PCP; asked her to call when he is discharged.

events.reason: Transitional care after hospital and rehab

documents.title: Transitional care visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
With daughter. Hospitalized 6/26 to 7/1 for central cord syndrome after a fall in the bathroom, then inpatient rehab until 7/18 (we have the hospital summary; rehab summary not received). Home now with home-health PT and OT twice weekly.

Now: hands stronger, buttons slow but possible, using built-up utensils. Burning across the shoulders much less. Collar off per rehab. Walking without device. No bladder trouble.

Meds reconciled: no changes from before admission.

Exam: vitals per flowsheet. Grip reduced both hands, finger dexterity slow; shoulder strength nearly normal. Legs strong. Mild left weakness as before. Systolic murmur. Lungs clear.

A/P:
1. Central cord syndrome, improving. Continue home PT/OT. Neurosurgery visit in August.
2. Falls: bathroom grab bars and shower chair ordered through home health; night lights; daughter checking daily, medical alert pendant discussed.
3. Chronic conditions stable; BMP, CBC today.
RTC October, sooner if needed.

documents.title: Follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
With daughter. Home PT/OT finished in September. Hands better; still drops small things and handwriting is shaky. Saw neurosurgery in August, told he is healing and to avoid falls; no letter here. Wearing a medical alert pendant. No falls since June. Eating well.

Exam: vitals per flowsheet. Grip mildly reduced both sides, improved from July. Mild left weakness. Gait steady, slower. Systolic murmur. Lungs clear.

Plan: A1c and BMP. Flu and COVID vaccines today. Continue current medicines. January visit with yearly labs.

documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Stable. Portal message to daughter.

documents.author: MA
documents.body: Pharmacy requests renewals for the blister-pack medications: hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg, metformin 500 mg, atorvastatin 20 mg. Loratadine OTC. Pended.

documents.body: Renewed, 30-day supplies with 11 refills, blister packaging.

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

documents.title: Follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
With daughter. Quiet winter, mostly indoors. No falls. Swallowing fine. Urine stream ok, up twice at night. Leuprolide continuing at urology. Daughter feels his memory has slipped a bit more since the summer; still safe alone during the day with her visits and the pendant, in her view.

Exam: vitals per flowsheet. Mild left weakness; grip slightly reduced both hands. Systolic murmur. Lungs clear. Feet intact skin and sensation.

Plan: yearly labs. Continue current regimen. Wellness visit April.

documents.title: Yearly labs
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: A1c in his range, kidneys stable, lipids and counts fine, urine albumin normal. Portal note to daughter.

documents.title: Refill question
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Daughter here. The pharmacy says his loratadine isn't on the blister pack. Can it be? Allergy season starts soon and he forgets the separate bottle.

documents.title: RE: Refill question
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Since he takes it only as needed, it stays as a separate bottle. A reminder on the blister card for allergy days may help; we asked the pharmacy to add a note to the label.

documents.title: Annual Wellness Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
WELLNESS VISIT with daughter.

Function: bathing with shower chair, dressing slowly (Velcro shoes), feeding himself. Daughter handles everything else. Lives alone with daily visits and the alert pendant. No falls since last June.
Cognition: Mini-Cog 0/3 today, clock disorganized; daughter confirms slow decline.
PHQ-9 4. Abstinent from alcohol.
Hearing aids in. Vision stable.
Advance care planning revisited: goals unchanged; MOLST still declined for now.
Vaccines up to date.

Exam: mild left weakness, reduced grip both hands, gait steady with care. Systolic murmur. Lungs clear.

Plan: follow-up in summer.

documents.author: urology
documents.body:
Dear colleague,

Mr. Fleming continues androgen deprivation with leuprolide every 3 months. PSA 0.6 today; 0.7 in November 2025. Stable, no rise. Voiding acceptable. Injection given. Next review in 6 months.

Urology

reports.text: Hyperdense crescentic extra-axial collection over the right frontoparietal convexity, maximal thickness 12 mm, with effacement of the adjacent sulci and 6 mm leftward midline shift. Basal cisterns patent. Old infarcts and chronic small-vessel change as before. No skull fracture.
reports.conclusion: Acute right frontoparietal subdural hematoma, 12 mm, with 6 mm midline shift.

documents.title: Hospital discharge summary
documents.author: neurosurgery
documents.body:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admitted 06/27/2026 via ED. Discharged 07/06/2026 to skilled nursing facility.

Presentation: 80-year-old man with multi-infarct dementia and central cord syndrome after a fall last year, brought in after his neighbor found him confused at home. He lives alone; he apparently fell several days ago, unwitnessed, and did not seek care. Over the last two days the neighbor noticed worsening headache, confusion and unsteadiness.

ED exam: drowsy, rouses to voice. Mild weakness and reduced sensation on the left. Pupils equal and reactive. No visible external injury.

CT head: acute right frontoparietal subdural hematoma, 12 mm, 6 mm midline shift.
Labs: counts, chemistries and coagulation normal; not on antithrombotic medication.

Course: admitted to neuro-ICU. Right craniotomy and evacuation of subdural hematoma 06/28/2026, uncomplicated. Alertness back to baseline by postoperative day 3 per daughter; headache resolved. Mild left weakness persists. Mobilized with PT, rolling walker. No seizures.

Diagnosis: acute traumatic subdural hematoma, evacuated.

Discharge medications: unchanged home medications (hydrochlorothiazide, metformin, atorvastatin, loratadine; leuprolide per urology).
Allergies: NKDA.

Follow-up: neurosurgery with CT head in about 6 weeks; staples removed at the facility; PCP after discharge from rehab.

Neurosurgery

documents.title: Discharge summary reviewed

documents.title: Daughter: admitted with brain bleed
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Daughter called. Saturday his neighbor found him confused at home; he must have fallen a few days before. CT showed bleeding on the brain, surgery yesterday to remove it. He is waking up more today and recognized her. Routed to PCP.

documents.title: PCP call back
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Spoke with daughter, supportive call. She is understandably shaken. Discussed that after rehab we should talk together about how much support he needs at home. She agrees.

events.reason: Transitional care after hospital and skilled nursing stay

documents.title: Transitional care visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
With daughter.

Interval: admitted 6/27 to 7/6 for an acute right subdural hematoma after an unwitnessed fall, evacuated by craniotomy 6/28. Skilled nursing rehab until 8/4 (their summary not yet here). Home since with home-health PT/OT and nursing.

Now: no headache. Back to his usual level of confusion per daughter, maybe a bit slower. Walks with a rolling walker indoors. Eating well but lost weight in the hospital. No falls since home. Daughter visits daily; pendant on.

Meds reconciled: home medicines resumed unchanged.

Exam: vitals per flowsheet, weight down. Healed right scalp incision. Alert, oriented to person. Mild left weakness; grip reduced both hands. Gait slow with walker. Systolic murmur. Lungs clear.

A/P:
1. Acute SDH, evacuated, recovering. Neurosurgery follow-up CT next week.
2. Falls with dementia, living alone: long talk with daughter about more support at home; she will look at options and we will talk again at the September visit.
3. Weight loss after admission: calorie-dense snacks; recheck next visit.
4. Chronic conditions: BMP and CBC today.
RTC September.

documents.title: Labs
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: BMP and CBC normal. Portal note to daughter.

documents.title: Skilled nursing facility discharge summary
documents.author: skilled nursing
documents.body:
SKILLED NURSING FACILITY DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Stay: 07/06/2026 to 08/04/2026

Admitted for rehabilitation after craniotomy for right subdural hematoma. Staples removed on day 10, incision healed. PT/OT daily: progressed from contact guard to supervision with a rolling walker; transfers independent. Cognition at baseline per family. No falls, no new medications. Weight trended down early, stable last two weeks.

Discharged home with daughter support and home-health services.

Skilled Nursing Facility

documents.title: SNF summary received
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: SNF summary received; matches daughter's account.

reports.text: Postoperative change of right craniotomy. Thin residual right frontoparietal subdural collection, smaller than on the preoperative study, without new hyperdense blood. No midline shift. Old infarcts and chronic small-vessel change unchanged.
reports.conclusion: Expected postoperative appearance with small residual right subdural collection; midline shift resolved.

documents.title: Neurosurgery follow-up
documents.author: neurosurgery
documents.body:
Dear colleague,

Seen 8/19 with his daughter, 7 weeks after right craniotomy for acute subdural hematoma. No headache; walking with a walker. Incision healed. Mild left weakness. CT today: thin residual collection, smaller, no new blood, midline shift resolved. No further imaging needed unless symptoms change. Fall prevention as discussed. Follow up with us as needed.

Neurosurgery
